The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y=f^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2, 0)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$
The point $B$ has coordinates $(0,2)$ and lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ If $f'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{2},$ what is $(f^{-1})'(0)?$
e-14720.worked_solution:
Since $B \,(0,2)$ lies on $f^{-1},$ we have $f^{-1}(0) = 2.$ We're also told that $f'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{2}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-14719.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
e-14719.problem: Consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2-3x}{4+5x}$ and the point $P\left(-1,-5\right)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point $\left(-5,-1\right).$
e-14719.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(-1, -5).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2-3x}{4+5x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{22}{(4+5x)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =-22\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(-1, -5)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(-5, -1)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ 

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(-5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-22)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{22}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14083756/assets/24d83be9fed627018111aff41b976881c98c6c58b2ceeb0ff11c033f9926afd3.png)

The figure above shows the graph of a piecewise linear function $y=f(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(3,2)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $(2,3)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x),$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2)?$
content.worked_solution:
Since $(2,3)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$
The slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ for $x\in [1,5]$ is $\frac{1}{2}$, hence, ${f}^{′}(3)=\frac{1}{2}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$

$$
